full_text:
Cross-benchers have slammed the Albanese government’s proposed overhaul of the NDIS as going “too far, too fast” as the changes to curb the growth of the $52bn program appear set to pass the parliament as early as next week.
The Greens and independent ACT senator, David Pocock, delivered scathing assessments of the bill they warn will enable blunt and indiscriminate cuts to individual budgets supporting more than 770,000 Australians with disabilities in a final Senate inquiry report released on Friday afternoon.
While the Labor-chaired committee recommended the bill pass, Greens senator Jordon Steele-John said the proposals would be “devastating to the lives of disabled people and their families”.
The bill forms part of the government’s plan to get the NDIS “back on track” and save $37.8bn over four years by tightening the eligibility criteria and subjecting all participants to independent functional assessments from 2028.
It will also give the NDIS minister, Mark Butler, the power to reduce funding categories for individuals by up to 99%. The government has already said it will apply a 50% reduction in individual participant budgets for social, civic and community participation.
Without the interventions, the government estimates the $52bn-a-year scheme will more than double in cost to $117bn a year in a decade’s time.
The Greens have acknowledged some changes should be made to make the NDIS work better for participants but suggested the scheme could be funded by a gas export tax.
“The choice that this Labor government is making is to rip life-changing supports away from disabled people instead of raising additional revenue through taxing gas exports shows their priorities clearly,” Steele-John wrote.
“This government is choosing the profits of large corporations over the lives of disabled people.”
Guardian Australia has previously reported that 241,000 NDIS participants will be shifted off the scheme by June 2031 after the introduction of the functional capacity test, to keep the number of participants at about 600,000.
During that period, an additional 105,000 will be stopped from entering the scheme.
Those shifted from the scheme are expected to be supported by programs run by states and territories with joint funding from the Commonwealth.
Pocock said no participant should be removed from the NDIS until those new programs are “funded, operating and accessible”, vowing to continue scrutiny of the changes.
“The true measure of these changes will be found in the experiences of people with disability. They must remain at the centre of what comes next,” Pocock said.
Coalition senators provided additional comments raising concerns that fraud and integrity within the NDIS had not been sufficiently addressed.
The government is expected to land a deal with the opposition early next week in order to pass the bill in the Senate.
Disability advocacy groups have been extremely critical of the government’s amendments to the NDIS, and have warned caring responsibilities will be shifted from the scheme to families, affecting women disproportionately.
Women With Disabilities Australia’s chief executive, Sophie Cusworth, said the government should deliver a comprehensive gender impact assessment of the bill.
“You cannot say you are working for women while looking to pass legislation that puts women’s safety, care, health and economic security at risk,” she said on Friday.
“That is not gender equality. That is neglect.”

title: Lending to property investors falls sharply in ‘tiny’ step towards fairer housing market in Australia, expert says
summary:
ABS data shows an almost 9% slump in new lending to investors after three interest rate hikes this year

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

In what one economist is describing as a “tiny step” toward a fairer housing market after decades of bad policy, property investors are shying away from established homes, and putting money into new builds instead, new data shows.

New lending to property investors fell sharply in the three months to June, slumping almost 9%, ABS data showed, while the number of total new home loans dropped by 5.4% in the June quarter.

Continue reading...
full_text:
In what one economist is describing as a “tiny step” toward a fairer housing market after decades of bad policy, property investors are shying away from established homes, and putting money into new builds instead, new data shows.
New lending to property investors fell sharply in the three months to June, slumping almost 9%, ABS data showed, while the number of total new home loans dropped by 5.4% in the June quarter.
The major banks have all reported a slump in mortgage applications in recent months, after three RBA official rate hikes and the federal budget’s investor tax changes that together have weighed on property prices.
The ABS’s head of finance statistics, Mish Tan, said: “lending fell across all borrower types this quarter and returned to similar levels to this time last year”.
Investor loans led the decline, falling by 8.6% in the June quarter after a 4.7% drop in the previous period. The number of investor loans was 2.8% higher than a year earlier, while the value of loans to investors was down by 10.2%.
The number of loans to first home buyers dropped by 2.9% over the three-month period, to be flat over the year.
Saul Eslake, a leading housing economist said the interest rates increases this year would be reducing the number of first home buyers..
“I don’t think it’s a cause for concern,” he said. “Whereas I would say the big fall in lending to investors for the purchase of established homes is actually something to be welcomed and celebrated.
“Because it means that prospective first home buyers are facing less competition from investors motivated by tax breaks for the housing we’ve already got.”
The number of loans to investors in established properties was down 14.8%, but the number of loans to investors buying new builds was up by 4.4% to a record high, a possible effect of the government’s budget carve-out for investor lending to build new housing.
Eslake said more investment in new builds actually increased rental supply, rather than pitting renters against investors for established housing.
He said these stats were a “tiny step” in the right direction to make Australia’s housing market more equal.
“A tiny step. But at least it is in that direction, whereas we’ve been taking tens of thousands of steps in the wrong direction for the last thirty years.”
National spokesperson for Everybody’s Home, Maiy Azize, said the figures show the governments tax reforms were “beginning to rebalance the market”.
“The most encouraging sign is that investors are pulling back from existing homes while investment in new housing is growing. That means less competition for first home buyers trying to buy a home,” Azize said.
“It also smashes the myth that immigration is the main driver of house prices. When governments change the rules and stop boosting investors, housing costs go down.
“Housing becoming more affordable is a good thing, especially for people trying to buy their first home.”

title: Teachers demand more scrutiny of Catholic school funding amid allegations of ‘sham arrangement’ with NSW Liberal group
summary:
Independent Education Union ‘deeply concerned … public funding for Catholic schools may have been wrongfully spent on Liberal party matters’

The union for independent school teachers in New South Wales has demanded greater scrutiny of Catholic schools as the chief executive of their governing body told a corruption inquiry payments to a lobbying firm were not a “sham arrangement” to fund Liberal party factional work.

Dallas McInerney insisted to the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Friday that Catholic Schools NSW funding wasn’t misused.

Continue reading...
full_text:
The union for independent school teachers in New South Wales has demanded greater scrutiny of Catholic schools as the chief executive of their governing body told a corruption inquiry payments to a lobbying firm were not a “sham arrangement” to fund Liberal party factional work.
Dallas McInerney insisted to the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Friday that Catholic Schools NSW funding wasn’t misused.
Icac is investigating whether McInerney arranged and approved illegal donations from the governing body for 600 Catholic schools to support alleged branch stacking efforts of the Christian factional group the Reformers.
The group wanted more conservative policies on issues such as abortion, euthanasia and same-sex marriage.
The inquiry has heard that Catholic Schools NSW paid Beckington, a lobbying company run by Reformers Christian Ellis and Jeremy Greenwood, $130,900 through invoices for consulting services between August 2019 and August 2021.
Greenwood’s company, JPG Advisory, was paid $135,000 between December 2021 and December 2023. The commission has heard that Reformers Robert Assaf and Dylan Whitelaw spent work hours on factional efforts while employed at Catholic Schools NSW.
On Friday, the Independent Education Union’s NSW branch, which had previously declined to comment while the inquiry was under way, said it was “deeply concerned by … [allegations] that public funding for Catholic schools may have been wrongfully spent on Liberal party matters”.
The IEU NSW/ACT branch secretary, Carol Matthews, said close scrutiny of public funding “was not applied to organisations such as Catholic Schools NSW that receive funding on behalf of Catholic diocesan schools”.
“Regardless of the findings of Icac in this matter, there should be greater scrutiny of bodies such as Catholic Schools NSW, which receive public funding on behalf of non-government schools,” Matthews said in a statement.
  About 80% of the funding distributed by Catholic Schools NSW comes from the state and federal governments. Government funding totalled about $3.8bn in 2024. The NSW premier, Chris Minns, has ruled out an independent audit of the schools governing body while Icac’s inquiry is under way.
McInerney stood aside from his role as CEO before the Icac hearings began “to allow the work of Catholic Schools NSW to continue its important mission”, he said in a statement previously. Catholic Schools NSW has previously said it “does not intend … to provide responses to questions that supersede the eight-week inquiry and legal process that is under way”.
McInerney on Friday was asked about messages in February 2021 between Assaf and fellow Reformer Jean-Claude Perrottet, the younger brother of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet, who is not accused of wrongdoing. Assaf and Jean-Claude were not directly employed by Beckington.
Jean-Claude Perrottet wrote to Assaf: “Ellis and I caught up with Dallas in Bowral to discuss money, had a long convo.”
The counsel assisting Juliet Curtin asked if the reason for Assaf and Jean-Claude’s interest was “because they knew that the arrangement in place was that you would pay Beckington money pursuant to a sham arrangement” – under which the money would come to them.
“No,” McInerney said on Friday. He said he could not recall the Bowral meeting. McInerney rejected evidence previously given by Assaf to the inquiry that Greenwood and McInerney met this year to discuss their summons.
The inquiry has previously heard that Jean-Claude Perrottet received money from Beckington. When the Catholic Schools NSW contract moved in 2021 from Beckington to JPG Advisory, Assaf and Jean-Claude allegedly each received a “kickback”, in Jean-Claude’s case, 50% of the monthly retainer, after he secured the contract with McInerney.
On Friday, McInerney repeatedly described Jean-Claude Perrottet as his “conduit” to Greenwood, who ran JPG.
Dylan Whitelaw, who worked at Beckington after being employed by McInerney at Catholic Schools NSW, has previously given evidence there was an arrangement under which payments from the schools’ governing body to Beckington were used to fund Reformers’ activities. McInerney repeatedly denied this.
McInerney was asked on Friday why Whitelaw, then only 21, was involved in negotiating an increase in Beckington’s retainer in 2021, and why McInerney cited Whitelaw’s departure from the company as a reason to end the contract with Beckington.
“I’m not confident they’ll have the in-house expertise to support our needs in the way DW [Dylan Whitelaw] has been,” McInerney wrote to a colleague.
On Friday, McInerney, who described Whitelaw as a “junior” at Beckington who carried out an “account manager” role and was responsible for “administrative interplay”, said his language had been consistent.
“Your in-house expertise as an account manager is … knowing the client, the rhythms, the relationships, how they service,” he said. The inquiry has previously heard that McInerney came to know Whitelaw through the Mittagoing Liberal branch after first meeting his parents. He employed Whitelaw at Catholic Schools NSW in 2019 after he graduated high school.
On Thursday, McInerney said correspondence leading up to the Beckington contract in which he told Ellis to get an ABN and a mailbox was “traditional due diligence”. He denied he was attempting to provide “a veneer of legitimacy” to the contract.
On Friday, the inquiry – and McInerney – learned that the ABN provided by Ellis in fact belonged to Ellis’s sister.
After Curtin suggested it showed due diligence “wasn’t particularly effective”, McInerney said: “I will add the point [that] I thought it was, but I’m happy to be enlightened”. The inquiry heard Beckington later wrote Catholic Schools NSW’s name incorrectly on invoices.
After Curtin suggested evidence of written work by Beckington was “de minimis”, apart from calendar entries for monthly meetings, McInerney insisted Beckington did consult for Catholic Schools NSW.
Asked if Beckington’s input was “only ever given orally”, McInerney said that Beckington had contributed to two “forward plans for public affairs and engagement in 2019” which involved “exhaustive planning sessions”.
The commission heard McInerney provided the two documents but there was no written evidence of Beckington being involved in the drafting process.
McInerney was expected to appear again before Icac next week.

title: Engine parts shattered Ryanair window that passenger was partly sucked out of, report says
summary:
Preliminary findings show fan blade broke off shortly after takeoff on 10 July flight from Greece to Germany

Broken engine parts were responsible for shattering a window on a Ryanair plane, causing a passenger to be partly sucked out mid-flight in July, US investigators have said.

A preliminary report by the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) found an engine fan blade broke off shortly after takeoff on the 10 July flight from Greece to Germany.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Broken engine parts were responsible for shattering a window on a Ryanair plane, causing a passenger to be partly sucked out mid-flight in July, US investigators have said.
A preliminary report by the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) found an engine fan blade broke off shortly after takeoff on the 10 July flight from Greece to Germany.
The Serbian entrepreneur Ljubisa Karović, sitting by the window in seat 11F, had his head and right arm sucked out of the broken window in the incident.
Karović was saved from being completely sucked out of the window by other passengers, who grabbed hold of him.
The 61-year-old told the Guardian he was lucky to be alive after the incident on Ryanair flight FR1879 and said his wife, Svetlana, told him he fainted several times, including after he had been pulled back inside the cabin.
The NTSB said the flight, which was scheduled to fly from Thessaloniki in Greece to Memmingen near Munich, “experienced a No 2 (right) engine fan-blade-out (FBO) failure during climb out from the Thessaloniki international airport (SKG), Thessaloniki, Greece”. The flight was operated by the budget airline’s subsidiary Malta Air.
Investigators found the cabin depressurised, and the two pilots decided to return to Thessaloniki airport, where they “made an uneventful landing”.
The NTSB was “delegated the investigation in full” by the Greek authorities a few days after the incident.
The flight crew’s timeline of the event was set out by the NTSB, detailing how they experienced a “high vibration” engine alert during the flight climb. They reduced the engine power in response and carried out a series of checks.
The engine vibration reduced and the crew continued the climb on autopilot. However, the vibrations then increased significantly and the crew heard a loud bang.
The flight crew put on their oxygen masks, declared an emergency and began an immediate descent.
The flight attendants reported “hearing and feeling a loud continuous vibration and seeing a small amount of fog/smoke before the oxygen masks dropped”, the report found.
Four bird strikes to the plane’s right engine were reported by flight crews in the 12 months preceding the incident, the report found, adding that bird remains were reportedly found in two of the cases. The fan blades had undergone ultrasonic inspections in recent months with “no findings”.
Karović told the Guardian less than a fortnight after the incident that he did not remember much, but had a painful head and neck. “It could have been the seatbelt, the fact that I was still strapped in. But maybe it is fate. I believe in God and I thank him every day,” he said.
The Boeing 737-800 plane had 149 passengers and four flight attendants on board.

title: ‘This is hell’: British widow ‘sick’ with worry over threat of being removed from Sweden
summary:
Joyce Thomas faces being forced to leave country after losing appeal against deportation

  • British widow, 78, told to leave Sweden under Brexit rules

The 78-year-old British widow threatened with removal from Sweden after 21 years has said she has been left feeling sick with worry after being told she had lost an appeal against deportation in a ongoing row over the country’s handling of Brexit.

“I am in shock. I feel sick. An individual’s life is at stake at my age. It is hell. I have done nothing wrong. I don’t take anything from this country. I am self sufficient, I put money in this country, have no criminal record,” said Joyce Thomas from her home in Sweden on Thursday.

Continue reading...
full_text:
The 78-year-old British widow threatened with removal from Sweden after 21 years has said she has been left feeling sick with worry after being told she had lost an appeal against deportation in a ongoing row over the country’s handling of Brexit.
“I am in shock. I feel sick. An individual’s life is at stake at my age. It is hell. I have done nothing wrong. I don’t take anything from this country. I am self sufficient, I put money in this country, have no criminal record,” said Joyce Thomas from her home in Sweden on Thursday.
Her plight, first revealed by the Guardian, has raised concerns in Brussels and in the UK about Sweden’s approach to the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, which was supposed to protect British nationals who lived in an EU member state before Brexit.
Earlier this week another family told how their father, a dementia patient in full-time care, was also threatened with removal after 25 years in Sweden.
The administrative court in Luleå upheld Sweden’s migration agency decision that Thomas was not eligible to stay because her application was made in 2023, after the cut-off date of December 2021.
Her legal representatives told the court in Luleå it was “not proportionate for her to be deported solely because she missed a deadline due to insufficient information. Furthermore, it is not acceptable that the Swedish authorities failed to inform her that she needed to file an application and of the deadline by which it was to be filed.”
Thomas now faces the prospect of a letter from the migration agency giving her four weeks to leave voluntarily , separating her from her son, her grandchildren, her network of friends, and away from her husband’s grave, which she regularly visits.
If she fails to comply, not only will she face a forced deportation, but the court of appeal has told her she could face a “re-entry ban” and “registered on a watchlist” preventing entry into a Schengen country, which includes Sweden “as long as the re-entry ban remains in effect”.
“No circumstances have come to light that would lead to a determination that, in your situation, you are particularly vulnerable,” the court ruling said noting that she had lived most of her life in the UK, had a pension from the UK and another son in the UK.
Thomas argued that after 21 years all her support network was in Sweden, with 23 people including doctors, priests and friends and fellow churchgoers writing to testify in support of her case.
“My friends, my husband’s burial place, grandchildren, everything is here, and to have to go and start again, it’s just unbelievable that at my age I’ve got to be uprooted for my home,” she said.
“This is hell. I get up in the morning, it’s in my head, I go to bed at night, it’s in my head. It’s horrible. I mean I have done nothing wrong. I am self sufficient. I put money in the country. I don’t take money out. I can’t comprehend this,” she added.
Her husband died in 2023 from cancer just four months after his last trip back to the UK to visit family. It was on the return that he learned from border officials that they had to make a special application to stay after Brexit.
Under article 18 of the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, late applications are permissible if there are “reasonable grounds” for doing so.
David Milstead, of the grassroots campaign group British in Sweden, said: “It would be difficult to find anyone who would argue that what is happening to Mrs Thomas and others in Sweden was an intended outcome of the withdrawal agreement. Problems will inevitably emerge when a new treaty is put into practice. However, the UK, EU and Sweden must act to address them. Words and expressions of concern won’t cut it.”
While the migration agency said not knowing an application was needed was not a “reasonable ground” for granting post-residency rights, Thomas is adamant neither she or her husband were notified that an application needed to be made before the end of 2021.
“The Swedish authorities have our ID cards, they have our emails, we heard nothing,” said Thomas.

summary: RedotPay’s US IPO has reportedly been delayed as it seeks regulatory approvals, while the company says it secured a US money transmitter license.
full_text:
RedotPay US IPO delayed amid regulatory, legal hurdles: Report
RedotPay’s US IPO has reportedly been delayed as it seeks regulatory approvals, while the company says it secured a US money transmitter license.
RedotPay’s plans for a US stock market debut have reportedly been delayed as the stablecoin payment company prepares to expand into the country.
The company delayed plans for a US initial public offering (IPO) while it seeks regulatory approvals and contends with legal disputes involving Binance, Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.
A RedotPay representative declined to comment on the timing of an IPO to Cointelegraph. The representative instead pointed to the company’s US expansion, saying RedotPay obtained a money transmitter license in the US this week and is preparing to launch its product in the country.
The reported setback follows a nearly $473 million lawsuit filed by Binance affiliates and comes as RedotPay works to expand its regulatory footprint in the US and other markets.
RedotPay’s IPO ambitions surfaced in February
RedotPay, founded in 2023 and based in Hong Kong, first emerged as a potential US public-market entrant in February, when reports surfaced that the company was considering a New York listing.
RedotPay has reportedly been working with JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs and Jefferies Financial Group on a listing that could raise more than $1 billion. At the time, the company was seeking a valuation of more than $4 billion.
Related: Bithumb sets 2028 IPO timetable as it overhauls internal controls
Separately, RedotPay has reportedly been in talks to raise up to $150 million in new funding amid organizational changes and preparations for a potential IPO. “As we transition from an early-stage startup to a unicorn, we are evolving our organizational structure and talent pool to support our ongoing growth trajectory,” RedotPay told Cointelegraph in March.
Binance lawsuit adds legal pressure
Binance affiliates sued RedotPay’s founders in Hong Kong earlier in August, seeking nearly $473 million in damages over allegations that they diverted hundreds of thousands of customers from Binance to RedotPay.
The plaintiffs allege that RedotPay’s founders used confidential information obtained through their previous work with Binance to build a competing payments business and attract Binance users. RedotPay rejected the allegations and told Cointelegraph it would “vigorously defend all claims.”
The dispute has also spilled into Singapore, where Binance and RedotPay disagree over the fate of a related case. RedotPay told Cointelegraph this week that it expected Binance to discontinue the case, while Binance rejected that account and said its claims remain active.

title: Crypto payments barely register among euro area merchants, ECB finds
summary: Crypto acceptance was just 0.2% online and remained below 1% at physical points of sale, while mobile payments gained ground.
full_text:
Crypto payments barely register among euro area merchants, ECB finds
Crypto acceptance was just 0.2% online and remained below 1% at physical points of sale, while mobile payments gained ground.
Crypto remains a marginal payment option among euro area businesses even as other forms of digital payments gain ground, according to a new European Central Bank (ECB) report.
Just 0.2% of companies selling goods and services online accept crypto assets, the ECB said in its survey on companies’ cash use, published Thursday. Cash remains the most widely accepted payment method, with 92% of companies with physical points of sale accepting it.
The ECB surveyed 8,205 businesses across the 21 euro area countries, covering retail, restaurants and cafes, hotels, and arts, entertainment and recreation. Market research firm Ipsos conducted the telephone interviews from Feb. 23 to April 10.
The findings come as the ECB advances work on a digital euro, a central bank digital currency (CBDC) designed to complement cash and preserve the euro’s role.
Mobile payments are catching up
Mobile payments recorded the biggest shift among payment methods at physical locations, with acceptance jumping to 68% in 2026 from 36% in 2024.
The most commonly accepted mobile options include instant payments and digital wallets, such as Apple Pay and Google Pay.
Acceptance of various payment instruments, 2024 versus 2026. Source: ECB
Cash edged up to 92% from 90%, while physical card acceptance rose to 88% from 87%. Crypto assets and stablecoins showed virtually no momentum at physical points of sale, remaining below 1% acceptance in both 2024 and 2026. Acceptance of bank checks, meanwhile, fell to 27% from 36%.
Merchants cite consumer preference as top payment factor
Consumer preference was the biggest factor companies considered when choosing which payment methods to accept, cited by 26% of respondents, followed by security at 22% and ease of handling at 15%.
Businesses that reject cash most often cited weak customer demand, at 36%, and difficulties depositing or withdrawing it, at 35%, while 29% pointed to security risks.
Most important criteria when choosing to accept a means of payment, euro area, 2026. Source: ECB
The longer-term outlook varies sharply by country, with 51% of cash-accepting small and medium-sized enterprises in Cyprus saying they may stop accepting cash, compared with 23% in Greece and 18% in Bulgaria.
What counts as accepting crypto?
The ECB survey asked companies whether they accept crypto assets or stablecoins, citing Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH) and Tether’s USDt (USDT) as examples.
Some crypto payment services allow merchants to receive settlement in traditional currency even when customers pay with crypto. The survey does not specify whether merchants should count such payments as crypto acceptance.
Related: Western Union brings stablecoin remittances to Visa network with Stablecard
Cointelegraph asked the ECB whether converted crypto payments could therefore go unreported by merchants and whether regulatory uncertainty could affect companies’ answers. The ECB said it “prefer[s] not to speculate.”
Asked whether euro area merchants are permitted to accept crypto under European Union rules, the ECB said it does not set payment regulation and referred Cointelegraph to the European Commission and national lawmakers.

title: Kalshi Ordered to Block Washington Bets Days After CFTC Backed It
summary: A King County judge gave the exchange until August 19 to stop offering sports, election and politics wagers in the state.
full_text:
In brief
- A Washington judge has ordered Kalshi to stop offering wagers on sports, elections, politics, entertainment, culture, tech and science, and "mentions" in the state.
- Kalshi must have an IP and residency geofence running by August 19, and a multi-source solution by September 2.
- The order lands two days after the CFTC used emergency powers to order the exchange to keep operating.
A King County Superior Court judge has issued a final order requiring Kalshi to shut down most of its Washington business, after finding the exchange likely broke the state's Gambling Act and Consumer Protection Act by running an illegal gambling operation, the state attorney general's office said on Thursday.
The order bars Kalshi from offering, accepting or facilitating wagers on sports, elections, politics, entertainment, culture, tech and science, and on "mentions," where users bet on whether a public figure will say particular words. It must have an IP address and residency-based geofence in place by August 19 and a multi-source geofencing system by September 2. The attorney general's office said the categories cover a substantial part of a business "increasingly driven" by sports.
Attorney General Nick Brown said Kalshi had "gotten rich promoting wagers on sports, elections, natural disasters" and events tied to the Iran war, adding that his office would keep holding the exchange to account.
The court also barred Kalshi from advertising the covered contracts in Washington, ruling that its marketing of illegal gambling amounted to "unfair and/or deceptive acts or practices." The state's complaint cites one Kalshi promotional tweet in which a person texts a friend to say they had "found a way to bet on the NFL even though we live in Washington," which the attorney general's office argues shows the company knew it was working around state law.
States versus CFTC
The ruling arrives two days after the Commodity Futures Trading Commission invoked emergency authority to order Kalshi to keep trading in line with the Commodity Exchange Act's core principles, acting on the exchange's own notification of a market emergency after New York sued it. The federal regulator's position is that event contracts are interstate derivatives beyond the reach of state gaming law, while Washington's is that each Kalshi bet stakes money on a contingent event and therefore meets the statutory definition of gambling.
The agency has sued nine states over the question, beginning with Illinois, Arizona and Connecticut and continuing through Wisconsin and Minnesota, which it sued within hours of that state's ban taking effect. President Donald Trump has backed the agency, calling state officials who oppose prediction markets "SCUM."
Kalshi has had less success in court than its federal ally. Thursday's order builds on a preliminary injunction granted in July, in which the judge found "substantial injury to Washington consumers" was likely without one, and the Washington Court of Appeals refused Kalshi's request to stay it.

full_text:
Across California, it’s time for Monterey Car Week, a cluster of events I once called “Comic-Con and the Oscars but with wheels.” For the last however many years, though, it’s mostly felt like an accumulation of rich people and influencers all crammed into the now-traffic-snarled peninsula, each paying 10 times the normal price for five-night minimums in three-star motels. While being there in person is pretty far down the list of things I want to do these days, that doesn’t mean there’s no interesting news coming out of the event. And no, I’m not talking about that hideous collaboration between Singer and Louis Vuitton. I’m instead referring to the latest creation from Czinger.
We first encountered Czinger’s direct-metal laser-sintering technology a decade ago, before founder Kevin Czinger had even started the car company—at the time, it was still Divergent 3D. But what better way to show to the rest of the automotive industry that they should contract with you as a parts supplier than by making your own car? That was the idea behind Czinger (the company), and it’s an approach that worked, as Divergent now has clients in the automotive sector as well as aerospace.
And what a car it is: a hybrid with tandem seating and an ability to set new lap records should you have the skill. But the performance is less interesting than the engineering. Free of its body panels, the structure looks more organic than mechanical, with topology-optimized shapes that are lighter but no less performing than traditionally designed alternatives.

title: Best Computer Monitors (2026): The Home Office Upgrade You Need
summary: My expert advice on what computer monitor to buy for your home office, ranging from budget-tier to fully featured.
full_text:
Most people never think about the monitor they use. But not you. If you work from home as I do, your monitor is your window into your trade, whether that's scrolling through endless spreadsheets or color grading short films. Different work has different needs, and finding the monitor that suits your specific use case can be tricky with all the options out there.
But with over a decade of testing and reviewing monitors under my belt, here are my recommendations on what you should buy today.
For more information, check out our guide to How to Choose a Monitor, as well as our recommendations for Best Gaming Monitors, Best Portable Monitors, and Best Cheap Monitors.
The Best Monitors for Your Home Office
It's worth spending more than a hundred bucks on your monitor. Whether it's to improve image quality, upgrade sharpness through higher resolutions, or to add extra ports, you'll want something that makes your daily work life more pleasant. That's why I recommend the Dell 27 Plus 4K as the monitor most people should buy. Unlike many 4K monitors, the Dell 27 Plus 4K sells for under $300 (oftentimes as low as $280), despite being quite bright and color-accurate for an IPS panel at this price. It even comes with a fast 120-Hz refresh rate. I like this feature, especially since higher refresh rates are becoming more commonplace on phone and laptop screens.
The only real downside to the Dell 27 Plus 4K is that the port selection is woefully limited. The two HDMI ports and one DisplayPort are enough for the basics, but if you have a laptop without HDMI, like a MacBook Air, you'll need a USB Hub or laptop docking station. For a more versatile monitor, I'd recommend upgrading to the model with a built-in USB hub (S2725QC). The QC model is identical, except that its extra USB ports make this monitor a far better fit for a connected home office. Dell does charge you $50 more for those ports, but for some, it'll be worth the convenience. Either way, you'll be hard-pressed to find a cheaper 4K monitor of this quality or a better monitor for under $300.
If you are looking for a larger, more fully featured home office monitor meant to sit at the center of a workstation, I'd recommend the Dell UltraSharp 32 4K (U3225Q). This thing is a beast. It's got just about every port and feature you can imagine, including a Thunderbolt-compatible USB-C port with power delivery up to 140 watts, an Ethernet jack, and a built-in KVM switch. This fully eliminates the need for a separate laptop docking station. Beyond that, it delivers on image quality in a big way. It uses IPS Black for enhanced color accuracy and contrast, and at the time of testing, it had the best image quality of any IPS display I'd tested.
It's not OLED, but the 120-Hz UltraSharp U3225Q is impressively bright in SDR, maxing out at well over 400 nits in my testing. You're paying a lot for the extra functionality and image quality, so make sure you actually need it before pulling the trigger on this over the 27-inch model.
There are plenty of 32-inch monitors out there if extra size is all you're looking for. Just remember, at 32 inches, anything under 4K isn't going to look sharp. But even 4K doesn't come close to the sharpness of something like a MacBook Pro. That's where the BenQ 27-inch 5K (MA270S) enters the picture. The combination of the 27-inch monitor and the 5K resolution (5120 x 2880) makes for one incredibly sharp display.
This BenQ monitor doesn't just match the MacBook Pro in pixel density. Using a device sync mode, it's designed specifically to be paired with a MacBook in terms of how the colors appear. Even some of the most expensive, high-end monitors designed for creators using Macs don't have that exact color match in how they're calibrated. BenQ has been refining this for years, and they have it nailed. It's all handled by software, which even lets you control the monitor's speaker volume right from your keyboard. I wish it could also control brightness, though.
But what's important is that when lined up next to a MacBook Pro, the colors are a perfect match. You can also use the sRGB color mode, which is how you get better color accuracy. That's what makes it such an incredibly powerful alternative to Apple's own Studio Display. While the Studio Display has fuller speakers and a slimmer design, it's certainly not worth the extra $500 in my mind. There's even a “nano gloss” texture option to match the Studio Display, which I'd recommend, as the glossy version I tested was highly reflective.
This isn't the only BenQ monitor made to match with Macs. The company also has the 27-inch 4K (MA270U), which gets you similar features with fewer pixels, but costs quite a bit less.
Cheap Monitors That Are Actually Good
I consider a budget monitor to be anything under $200, and you'll find dozens and dozens of these hanging out at Amazon or Best Buy. But many are old. Many have poor colors. It's trickier to find some newer models that are actually worth the money. I wasn't surprised to see that the Dell 27 Plus ranked among the very highest in my testing. It only costs $150, but it delivers really strong 1080p performance in terms of colors and brightness.
The most surprising feature of this monitor is its 144-Hz refresh rate. The smooth motion really gives the monitor the premium feel that monitors at this price lack, and it also comes with all the same adjustability features and an integrated VESA mount on the back. Put this on your desk, and aside from the resolution, you'll never think of it as a “budget” monitor.
But maybe you want to keep things even cheaper. No problem. While a monitor under $100 is going to have some flaws, I found a decent one in the MSI Pro MP243W E14. It stands out in the thing that matters most: image quality. I measured 359 nits at its brightest, and the color coverage is surprisingly good, both in terms of saturation and accuracy. It even has a 144-Hz refresh rate, which means it can double as a cheap gaming monitor when it needs to. I also like the design, which offers thin bezels around the display and an all-white exterior. Its flaws, however, include the lack of ports and adjustments. It can only tilt slightly. It's only 24 inches, which will likely feel small for most people.
I was also really surprised by the upgraded version of this monitor, the MP273QW E14. Rather than being stuck at 1080p, this model gives you a sharper image with a resolution of 2560 x 1440. While it has the same lack of adjustment, it is a more standard 27-inch size and delivers even better overall image quality.
Faster, Smarter, and More Extreme
This monitor is one of the favorites I've tested in the past couple of years. It was among the first QD-OLED monitors designed for content creation and entertainment. While there are a couple of options out there today from companies like Asus, the Dell 32 Plus 4K opens up the brilliant image quality of OLED to an entirely new audience. One reason high-quality HDR video is scarce is the lack of affordable screens to watch and edit it on. With this monitor out in the world, though, there's no excuse. It even has a 120-Hz refresh rate and plenty of ports. The combination of OLED's fast response time and the faster refresh rate makes this a solid gaming monitor in your off hours. I haven't included gaming monitors in this guide, primarily because they're an entirely different beast. Check our recommendations of the Best Gaming Monitors for some recommendations on that front.
But if you're really serious about creating professional, HDR video, there's still nothing else on the market quite like the Studio Display XDR. We all waited a long time for Apple to revisit the Studio Display, and while the monitor we eventually got was a bit less ambitious in scope than we all hoped, this 27-inch 5K Mini-LED monitor is the new king in HDR performance. It has 2,304 dimming zones, and according to my testing, it could do 1,905 peak HDR brightness in a 25-percent window. C

title: Her Brain Was Broken. It Was Fixed With Sound—Not a Scalpel
summary: One woman’s meth addiction was so bad, the only option left might have been brain surgery. Then a single session of noninvasive, focused ultrasound seemed to do what years of treatment could not.
full_text:
Erin McNulty had been missing for weeks when her mother, Linda, sat down on a chair in her living room, exhausted. Linda had put in her usual seven-day workweek at the antiques shop she runs near Burlington, Vermont. She’d spent her free evenings driving around, trying to track down her daughter. Erin, 45 at the time, had been using methamphetamine for years.
Her substance use started in high school—first alcohol, then marijuana, and eventually heroin. Erin’s brother used heroin, too. When Linda found out, she started driving her kids to a methadone clinic three hours away in Massachusetts. The methadone helped, but it made Erin feel tired all the time, so she started using cocaine to stay awake. There were stretches of sobriety—she had her daughter during one of them, in 2008. The family took trips to the Great Escape waterpark in New York and Hampton Beach in New Hampshire. There were also several overdoses and attempts at rehab. Eventually, Erin switched to suboxone and stopped using heroin. But when a friend introduced her to meth, Linda says, “Erin was gone.”
Linda turned on the TV and was flipping through the channels when a 60 Minutes segment caught her attention. It was early 2024, and the show focused on a procedure that might help people with substance use disorders. Linda immediately thought of her daughter. The procedure involved beaming ultrasound through the skull to treat the brain. Researchers at West Virginia University were testing it on people with Alzheimer’s disease and addiction.
The neurosurgeon behind the procedure, Ali Rezai, was a pioneer in the field of deep brain stimulation, which involves cutting into the skull to implant electrodes that can reach neurons deep in the brain. He was excited by the ability of ultrasound—the imaging tool best known for observing fetal development during pregnancy—to reach into the same brain structures without breaking the skin. There would be no drilling into the skull, no poking or prodding the brain’s delicate tissue. The ultrasound could be delivered in 20 minutes, and patients could go home the same day.
Linda couldn’t believe what she was seeing on TV. She yelled out to her teenage granddaughter, Erin’s child, to come watch. “Look at this doctor,” she said. “They’re fixing people!” It didn’t matter that the trial was happening more than 600 miles away. She was going to get Erin to West Virginia. But first she had to find her.
Rezai, who was born in Iran, grew up in Los Angeles, and completed his neurosurgical training in New York, never expected to end up in West Virginia. “My colleagues said, ‘You’re committing academic suicide,’” he says. But Rezai saw an opportunity to pursue new treatments at the epicenter of the US addiction crisis. Almost 45 million Americans meet the criteria for a substance use disorder, and although drug overdose deaths in the US have been declining for the past three years, there were nearly 70,000 such deaths in 2025. West Virginia has the highest rate of overdose deaths in the country by population, more than double the national average.
Over the course of his 30-year career, Rezai has carried out more than 3,000 deep brain stimulation surgeries. (He stopped counting after that.) He’s used the approach to treat Parkinson’s, severe obsessive-compulsive disorder, traumatic brain injury, and more recently, opioid addiction. His first DBS operation, during his medical residency at New York University in 1996, took a painstaking 16 hours. Dozens of computers were crammed into a basement room to record from the patient’s brain. Rezai says they had to operate in the basement because of all the beeping, clicking, and whirring. Today, these devices can be implanted in a fraction of the time with just a few computers—but brain surgery is still brain surgery.
The first attempts to harness ultrasound to treat the brain required brain surgery too. In the 1950s, brothers William and Francis Fry built a system that could focus ultrasound beams into a single point, similar to how a magnifying glass can focus scattered sunlight. The whole apparatus took up two rooms, with the controls upstairs and the ultrasound probes coming through the ceiling. Ultrasound waves generate heat at high intensities, and the brothers used their system to burn pinprick-sized lesions in the brains of animals without damaging surrounding tissue. They did the same in patients with Parkinson’s disease to destroy tiny portions of brain tissue responsible for abnormal movement. It relieved people’s tremors, but the procedure never caught on because it required removing part of the skull. By the 1970s, the drug levodopa became commercially available to treat Parkinson’s, making surgery an unnecessary risk.
Modern focused ultrasound machines can emit dozens of beams from different angles through an intact skull. When an electric voltage hits their piezoelectric crystals, they vibrate rapidly, producing high-frequency sound waves. With the click of a mouse, the waves can be targeted to a spot in the body with millimeter precision. On their own, individual beams don’t produce enough energy to affect the bone or tissue they pass through. But when they converge into a single point at the targeted depth, they reach their maximum intensity.
High-intensity ultrasound, like what the Fry brothers used, is already approved to treat a handful of conditions, including uterine fibroids, certain kinds of prostate cancer, and symptoms of Parkinson’s that can’t be treated with drugs. But ultrasound can also be delivered in low intensities to alter neural activity in the brain.
The ability to get deep into the brain without holes or incisions is why Rezai and others are so excited about ultrasound. Other types of noninvasive stimulation, such as transcranial magnetic stimulation, only breach the outer layers of the brain. They can’t penetrate the nucleus accumbens, the pea-sized part of the brain Rezai is targeting for addiction. Rezai wanted to see if focused ultrasound could.
In 2021, with permission from the Food and Drug Administration, Rezai and his team at WVU launched an exploratory trial to test the safety of focused ultrasound in volunteers with addiction. They used an FDA-approved machine designed to emit high-intensity waves but turned the power way down, starting off with a low dose and gradually increasing it.
Rezai had no idea how long the effects of a one-time ultrasound procedure might last. Almost immediately, the approach showed promise. “The cravings went down live on the table,” he says. The volunteers started to report feeling, well, different.
With the TV segment on Rezai occupying her thoughts, Linda intensified her efforts to find Erin. A few days later, Linda found her in a hotel in downtown Burlington. Erin had been staying with an ex-boyfriend. “She was in pretty rough condition,” Linda says.
She brought Erin home to their house in the country and told her about the study. Erin watched the video over and over. She felt hopeful, but she was also scared. She had experienced anxiety and depression for much of her life, and drugs were a way to cope. She felt her most normal when she was taking drugs, which is what kept her using.
“It absolutely took over,” Erin says. “I couldn’t get out of it.” The drive to get meth overrode everything else in her life, including being a mother and putting a roof over her head. She wanted to get better, but she couldn’t imagine not doing meth anymore.
Linda was convinced that Rezai’s study was her daughter’s way out. To be considered, Erin needed to be in active treatment within the WVU Medicine system. Linda planned to fly with her daughter and granddaughter to Pittsburgh, the closest major airport to Morgantown, and drive the rest of the way, about an hour and a half. But it took three tries to get Erin on the plane. Their first flight was early in the morning, and they didn’t make it to the airport on time. During the second attempt, they were waiting to boa

title: This Art Project Slows Down Citi Bikes to Make NYC’s Rent Crisis Feel Real
summary: Ground Truth makes the shared rental bikes harder to pedal through rent-burdened neighborhoods, offering a tangible way for people to experience income inequality.
full_text:
Justin Blinder lost his job two weeks before the Covid-19 pandemic hit in 2020. To pay his rent, he turned to delivery services, riding his bicycle across New York City to deliver food. As he went, he noticed the disparities in where the food items went. Which order of Nomé sushi went where and how much people tipped.
“The city started to feel much more economically and psychologically disparate,” Blinder tells WIRED. “It really changed so much on a block-by-block level. These inequalities and demographic differences were happening in such close proximity.”
That experience has morphed into an art-project gadget called Ground Truth that Blinder hopes will raise awareness about the housing affordability crisis in New York City and beyond by making a Citi Bike—one of the ever-present ebike rental options across the city—harder to ride through places where it’s harder to live.
Blinder, a Brooklyn artist and contractor at Meta, received a $10,000 grant for the project from a Brooklyn arts organization called Idle Hands.
Ground Truth is a box that will trigger the brakes on the Lyft-owned bicycle, adding more resistance to the pedals when riding through rent-burdened neighborhoods, where people living in those areas spend more than 30 percent of their income on rent. Ride past an economically well-off block, and the bike is easier to pedal. Going past a block where rent takes the bulk of the households’ incomes can slow the bike down to a crawl.
There are two versions, one that can work on a regular bicycle and one built specifically for Citi Bikes.
The box mounts on the bike’s fork and is then attached to the front brake line. A battery-powered GPS component tracks the bike’s location. As it moves, the location is cross-referenced with household economic data from the US Census Bureau’s American Community Survey, stored on the device. When the bike passes a block the dataset says has a higher percentage of rent insecurity, the microcontroller triggers a small motor that applies the brake to add resistance, and the bike gets physically harder to pedal.
Blinder is also the creator of the Covid-inspired Pandemic Pulse, an app that used real time Covid statistics to change the brightness of your device’s screen. The screen would darken whenever data showed infections growing, and then black out briefly whenever a death was recorded. As with Ground Truth, Blinder says the goal of these projects is to help people understand large datasets in a more tactile way.
“It’s really trying to make the way we traditionally visualize a lot of big data more tangible and embodied,” he says. “Create something a bit more confrontational and try to force people to consider how they traditionally look at data.”
Blinder says the device is not a working product or something other people will be able to use. (Likely for legal reasons, as you can’t just change how a rideshare electric bicycle drives.) But he has ridden about 35 miles or so, filming the experience as Ground Truth changes its resistance in different communities.
He hopes the project will also call attention to the rising cost of renting a Citi Bike. The service has raised its prices for the past five years in a row.
“The price has just become so astronomical that it felt like this really nice connective tissue in the affordability crisis, connecting all of those different elements,” Blinder says. “It’s really thinking about how affordability changes throughout the city on a block-by-block basis and how this system could allow people to experience that.”

title: Dell XPS 13 Review: Move Over, Neo
summary: It’s amazing how few compromises Dell made to get the new XPS 13 down to $700, but I strongly recommend the $900 model, which comes with 16 GB of RAM.
full_text:
The display is gorgeous. Excellent touchpad and backlit keyboard. Decent battery life and performance. Charges from both sides. 16-GB model available, unlike MacBook Neo.
TIRED
8 GB of RAM in base model is just not enough. No headphone jack.
It’s hard to talk about the new Dell XPS 13 without mentioning the MacBook Neo. To say it takes inspiration from the choices of its rival would be an understatement—whether that’s the type of processor, the quality of the display, or the amount of memory.
But don’t think that’s a bad thing. The Dell XPS 13 feels different from other Windows laptops you can buy for $700 (or $900 for the better configuration), and a lot of that is for the better. I have some beef with this laptop's starting configuration, but I also can’t deny what makes it so compelling and unique, even among the very best laptops you can buy.
Incredible Value
The MacBook Neo did one thing very well: translate what people love about MacBooks into a $700 package (or $600 at the time it was announced). In terms of the things you can touch and feel, the MacBook Neo is every bit as premium-feeling as a MacBook Air. The materials used in the chassis, the quality of the keyboard and trackpad, and the caliber of the display—none of it has the “budget device” stink. There's more to the story of the MacBook Neo than that, but you can tell it’s how Apple made decisions on which features to cut or compromise on.
Unlike nearly every Windows laptop selling for under $1,000, the Dell XPS 13 takes that same approach. Even the base configuration comes with a 2560 x 1600-resolution touch display with a 120-Hz refresh rate, up to 427 nits, and excellent color reproduction. The touchpad is glass and feels excellent to use. In terms of build quality, it’s top-tier. It’s made out of aluminum, and there’s no flexing to be heard of in the chassis. It opens with one finger, and the hinge doesn’t wobble. The bezels around the display are tiny, giving it a very modern look. It’s also incredibly thin at just half an inch thick, matching the MacBook Neo. That’s all very attractive stuff that makes a strong first impression when handling the device for the first time.
Here are some things the new Dell XPS 13 has that the Neo doesn’t:
A touchscreen display
A 120-Hz refresh rate
A backlit keyboard
Two up-to-date, 10-Gbps USB ports (one on each side!)
Support for two 4K monitors (or three if the lid is closed)
Fast storage speed
The one thing it’s missing is a headphone jack. The MacBook Neo includes one, and I do think that’s an unfortunate miss. But I really appreciate that Dell didn’t skimp on port quality. There’s one USB-C port on each side of the device, both of which can support a 4K display simultaneously at 60 Hz, charge the device, or transfer files at 10 Gbps.
While the speakers aren’t what I’d call good, Dell did throw in two tweeters for 8 watts of output. They’re at least on par with the Neo. It's the same story with the 1080p webcam. The addition of an IR camera for Windows Hello login is appreciated.
So, with all that, you might be wondering how Dell is getting away with selling the XPS 13 for a starting price of $700. There's a catch, as always.
More Memory Please
Dell made two significant compromises to reduce the price of the XPS 13. First, it uses a lower-powered Intel processor, the Core 5 320. Dell is surely saving money on this six-core chip, but to my surprise, I was impressed by this modest little piece of silicon. The XPS 13 is one of the first laptops to use this chip, which is part of the new Intel Wildcat Lake line. There are some other laptops coming out with this chip, meant to compete with the Apple A18 Pro used in the MacBook Neo and the Qualcomm Snapdragon X. The Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3i is one such option, which uses the Intel Core 7 350, but as a 16-inch laptop, it's hardly a competitor to the highly compact XPS 13.
But really, there’s plenty of performance here for what the device is intended to be used for. The Core 5 320's raw single-core performance and graphics aren’t as strong as the A18 Pro, but in terms of multicore performance, it’s much more powerful. Then, there's the battery life. You're not getting quite as much as the MacBook Neo, but I was satisfied being able to stay away from the outlet all day and still last 15 hours in local video playback.
Memory is the other major area of compromise, and it’s where my concerns lie. The $700 model starts with only 8 GB of RAM, which is what I tested. This is rare these days. You’d have to be shopping in the sub-$500 category to find an 8-GB Windows laptop, which puts the $700 Dell XPS 13 in perspective. It’s a more premium laptop than you could ever find at that price in terms of build quality, display, trackpad, and keyboard. But it’s actually quite expensive for the amount of memory you get. Fortunately, Dell includes 512 GB of storage in all the models, which is also an important consideration when evaluating the price. While it was originally stated that the device would be configurable up to 1 TB of storage, right now you're maxed out at 512 GB.
But maybe you’re wondering whether you really need 16 GB of RAM. After all, five years ago, it was the default on laptops at this price. I was curious how well an 8-GB model could handle multitasking. Outside of the MacBook Neo, I haven’t used an 8-GB laptop in a long time, as even budget-level Windows machines have come with 16 GB of RAM over the past few years.
The RAM limitation was much worse than I even expected. Performance generally starts to slow when you’re using 80 percent of the available memory. At idle, with no open applications, Windows 11 was using well over 80 percent of memory due to background processes. Ending the background tasks that Microsoft Edge is always running brought that down to 70 to 75 percent, but Search alone was taking somewhere between 150 and 190 megabytes of memory at all times. That’s not Dell’s fault, but there’s a reason Microsoft has been pushing for broader acceptance of 16 GB of RAM as a base. More AI functionality means more background tasks running at all times, which drastically eats up your available memory.
Ten tabs in Chrome put this dangerously close to maxing out the memory. You get spikes up to over 95 percent at times. As you can imagine, getting the Dell XPS 13 to use up nearly 100 percent of the available memory took almost no effort at all. Just play one YouTube video in the background while keeping a handful of browser tabs open. A laptop that feels sluggish with just a few browser tabs open is acceptable for a laptop that costs $300. But it’s questionable, given that Dell is selling this device for $700. Regardless of how pretty and portable the design is, I would only recommend this version of the laptop for those with fairly minor computing needs. You don't want this if you're using it for most of your day.
That wasn’t quite my verdict, however, about the MacBook Neo. And I promise: That’s not because I’m biased against Windows. Apple has taken a lot of flak over the years for suggesting that 8 GB of RAM on a Mac is equivalent to 16 GB on Windows. That’s an exaggeration, but it is true that it takes a bit more to slow down the MacBook Neo. I pulled up the same exact series of tabs in Google Chrome, and the Neo experienced less lag and choppiness. Neither is meant for professionals, but it's worth mentioning since Dell is trying to position the XPS 13 directly against the MacBook Neo.
There's Good News
Here’s the upside: Unlike Apple, Dell does sell a 16-GB model. It’s a $200 increase, but it takes the XPS 13 from being disappointing to something incredibly solid. I can’t, in good faith, recommend that most people buy the $699 model that comes with only 8 GB of RAM. But as a $900 laptop with 16 GB of RAM, the Dell XPS 13 is excellent. In fact, it just might be the best laptop you can buy under $1,000. It’s $100 more than the MacBook Neo with 512 GB of storage, but it’s the superior lapt

title: The Real Reason Data Center Gas Power Plants Are So Dirty
summary: A massive new gas plant in Texas will be built with much less efficient technology than regular gas plants. It’s far from the only data center power project to rely on dirty turbines.
full_text:
Amazon has acquired a massive off-grid power plant being built in Texas for one of its data centers that could be one of the biggest sources of greenhouse gas emissions in the US.
But size isn’t the only reason its climate toll will be so high. The plant will rely on a much less efficient set of gas turbines than regular power plants use; these kinds of turbines are also increasingly being put to use at other data center projects around the US. That could have big implications for the environmental impact of artificial intelligence—and the future of the US grid.
Amazon’s Texas power plant is permitted to emit up to 33 million tons of greenhouse gases a year. The project will rely solely on simple cycle turbines, which mix fuel and air in a combustion chamber to create energy, letting off a significant amount of waste heat in the process. Combined cycle units, which are generally used at on-grid power plants, add an additional steam turbine component to capture the waste heat and turn it into more energy. That means they release fewer emissions for the same amount of energy.
Permitted emissions on natural gas plants are usually much higher than their actual emissions. But even if Amazon’s facility emits half of what’s on the permit each year, it would still create more greenhouse gas pollution than 78 average-sized natural gas plants, according to the US Environmental Protection Agency.
The Texas plant provides “on-site generation that won't raise electricity costs for Texas families,” Amazon spokesperson Heather Callahan writes in an email to WIRED, adding that the site would also have solar and battery storage and that the company is still committed to reaching net-zero emissions by 2040.
Using simple-cycle turbines is becoming an increasingly common practice for data center power developers looking for flexible power that’s quick to install. At least three power plants being developed in Ohio by oil and gas company Williams for Meta will also rely on simple cycle units, according to permit applications. In Abilene, Texas, Crusoe is building a power plant on its Stargate campus to power a Microsoft data center with 39 simple-cycle turbines. The permit application for Google’s Goodnight data center at another Texas site being developed by Crusoe describes relying on 20 simple-cycle turbines. And both xAI’s Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 data centers in Memphis are being powered by dozens of simple cycle turbines. All of them are permitted to release millions of tons of greenhouse gases. (Both Williams and Crusoe tell WIRED in an email that their gas plants comply with local and national regulations and are outfitted with emissions control technology.)
Britt Burt, a senior vice president at Industrial Info Resources, an energy market intelligence firm, says that he didn’t expect data center developers to lean so heavily on simple cycle turbines for power.
“It’s not the most efficient way to use a gas turbine,” he says.
For companies racing to get data centers online, though, it’s a lot quicker—and cheaper—to install a handful of simple-cycle turbines than wait for the additional equipment needed for combined-cycle units, especially given a yearslong backlog for turbine orders and associated parts.
“Right now, because of the way the supply chain is for turbines, they’re having to go with what they can get their hands on,” says Burt.
Then there’s the energy needs of data centers, especially those training AI models. Thanks to their fewer moving parts, simple cycle turbines can start up and shut down more rapidly than combined cycle units. That suits AI training, which requires big spikes of energy on demand. (In fact, those spikes are so big that many data center operators have reported turbines breaking thanks to the extreme stress of turning on and off.)
“If you have a highly fluctuating load, it's better to have 30 things that can individually turn on and off than to have one giant thing that doesn't like to be turned on and off,” says Stephen Lynch, a professor of mechanical engineering at Penn State and director of the school’s Center for Gas Turbine Research, Education, and Outreach.
Simple cycle turbines also generally don’t require water, which itself is an increasingly hot-button issue for communities near data centers. Burt estimates that a 250-megawatt combined-cycle plant could use about 75,000 gallons per hour. The permit application for the new Amazon plant specifically lists simple cycle technology’s lack of water use as an “environmental benefit.”
The federal government and a growing number of state governors across the political spectrum are encouraging data center power providers to bring or build their own energy to avoid raising consumer electric bills.
Some companies have promised to integrate their power plants with the grid eventually. Callahan, the Amazon spokesperson, said that the Texas plant is “designed to transition to grid-connected service as interconnection timelines allow.” Williams told WIRED earlier this month that it may consider the Ohio plants for interconnection in the future.
There are power plants designed with simple-cycle turbines, known as peaker plants, which are used to rapidly provide power to the grid when demand is high. But for now, the rapid construction of new islanded power plants with inefficient turbines—many of which are designed to last for decades—threatens to create a parallel fossil fuel grid that generates millions of tons of greenhouse gas emissions.
If the AI bubble bursts or tech companies’ energy needs dip, though, it’s possible that the massive, inefficient gas plants could no longer have a purpose.
“We call that a stranded asset,” Burt says, chuckling.

title: 白宮報告《中國洗產地大計劃》：台灣與日韓同列 40 多國第一梯隊
summary:
白宮貿易與製造業政策辦公室 8 月 13 日發布 25 頁報告《The Great Transshipment […]

〈白宮報告《中國洗產地大計劃》：台灣與日韓同列 40 多國第一梯隊〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
白宮貿易與製造業政策辦公室 8 月 13 日發布 25 頁報告《The Great Transshipment Scam》，指控中國透過 40 多個國家洗產地規避關稅，年規模估在 400 億到 3,030 億美元之間。報告把這些國家分成三個梯隊，台灣與日本、南韓、加拿大、歐盟同列第一梯隊。報告同時載明，五份估算不能相加、也不能直接比較。
（前情提要：川普鎖喉半導體命脈，傳多晶矽將開徵 15% 關稅、加設進口地板價）
（背景補充：台灣人涉嫌走私 Nvidia AI 晶片到中國！彭博：利用「日本當跳板」偷運美超微高階伺服器）
重點摘要
- 白宮報告把 40 多國分成三梯隊，台灣列 Tier 1，與日韓、歐盟、加拿大、印度、以色列、墨西哥同層
- 五份估算從高盛的 400 億美元到 Altana 的 3,030 億美元，差距達 7.5 倍
- 以 750 億美元中位情境推估，年減 GDP 1,130 億到 1,500 億美元、45 萬個工作被排擠
白宮貿易與製造業政策辦公室（OTMP）8 月 13 日發布一份 25 頁報告，標題直接叫《The Great Transshipment Scam》，中文可以理解成「洗產地大騙局」。報告指控中國透過 40 多個國家把商品換上新國籍再送進美國，藉此避開高關稅。
這份報告由川普的貿易顧問 Peter Navarro 領軍的辦公室產出，他把中國轉運的商業邏輯講得很直白。
轉運背後的驅動力是關稅套利。當一件商品從甲國出口到美國要付的關稅，高於從乙國出口，這個價差就變成獲利機會，甚至本身就變成一門生意。
台灣被列第一梯隊，跟日韓歐盟同層
報告把這 40 多個國家分成三個梯隊，台灣出現在 Tier 1。
Tier 1 叫「多元化規模領先者」（Diversified Scale Leaders），成員是加拿大、歐盟、印度、以色列、日本、墨西哥、南韓與台灣。報告對這一層的定義是：中國關聯商品的絕對數量大，但這些國家本身工業基礎多元、也是對美出口的主要平台，因此轉運風險是「嵌在大量合法貿易流之中」。
這個措辭跟 Tier 2 明顯不同。Tier 2 是「與中國有顯著經濟整合的規模領先者」，成員是巴西、印尼、馬來西亞、泰國、土耳其與越南，報告直指越南、泰國、馬來西亞與印尼已經深度嵌進中國周邊的製造網路，成為電子、機械、塑膠、鞋類、成衣與零組件的主要平台。
Tier 3 是國家數量最多的一層，叫「小型機會主義目標」，靠的是低成本勞力、自由區、保稅倉儲或執法能量不足。柬埔寨提供低成本勞力與出口加工區，寮國與緬甸提供中國周邊的邊境走廊，巴拿馬與哥斯大黎加提供海運與再出口平台，亞塞拜然與喬治亞提供鐵路與內陸港轉運，約旦則靠優惠貿易准入與利基組裝能力。
五份估算差了 7.5 倍
報告最引人注目的是那個 400 億到 3,030 億美元的區間，但這個區間其實是五份不同來源的估算並排放在一起。
- 高盛（Goldman Sachs）: 約 400 億美元，範圍最窄，只抓純粹的改道轉運
- 白宮經濟顧問委員會（CEA）: 342 億到 896 億美元，報告採用中點 600 億美元
- Exiger（AI 供應鏈公司）: 約 750 億美元，以產品層級與貨運流分析為基礎
- 商務部貿易與經濟分析辦公室（OTEA）: 1,090 億美元的貿易轉移基準，涵蓋 459 個 HS6 產品類別；另單獨估算 2025 年經主要樞紐轉運約 670 億美元
- Altana: 3,030 億美元，屬於設施層級的曝險上限值
報告在同一段白紙黑字寫著，這些估算「不可相加，也不能直接比較」，因為各自的資料集、方法論、產品篩選與轉運定義都不一樣。把最高的 3,030 億拿來當結論，跟把最低的 400 億拿來當結論，都不是報告的原意。
經濟衝擊的推估同樣有前提，以 750 億美元的中位情境計算，報告估算美國因為中國產品洗產地，年減 GDP 1,130 億到 1,500 億美元、45 萬個工作被排擠、聯邦稅收短收 190 億到 260 億美元。
報告註明，這 45 萬是模型推估的數字，不是實際觀察到的失業人數，用途是說明曝險的量級。關稅收入損失則抓 100 億到超過 1,000 億美元，取決於用 25%、35% 還是 45% 的關稅價差去算。
AI 查緝將上場
美國執法端已經動起來，互惠貿易協定裡加進了防止利益外溢到第三國的條款，行政命令 14411 則從進口商責任、保證金、國內資產、股權揭露、關係企業與罰則等面向強化海關執法。
報告另外描繪了一套叫「Detective Border」的 AI 系統，要串起貨運資料、routing 紀錄、產品分類、股權關係、產能指標、異常偵測與電腦視覺，協助美國海關暨邊境保護局（CBP）分辨什麼是正當的近岸外包與外人投資，什麼是純粹的借道通關。
不過報告結尾自己踩了煞車，直說「現在要判斷本屆政府關稅與反轉運政策的淨效果還太早」，因為貿易與海關數據有時間落差，好幾項執法條款也還在落地中。
常見問題
台灣被白宮列入洗產地名單，代表台灣被指控違規嗎？
不完全是。台灣被列在 Tier 1「多元化規模領先者」，報告的定義是這類國家對美出口量大、工業基礎多元，轉運風險夾雜在大量合法貿易之中，與 Tier 2 的「與中國深度整合」屬於不同性質的描述。
報告說的損失到底是 400 億還是 3,030 億美元？
兩者都是，但來自不同機構與方法。高盛只算純改道轉運得出 400 億美元，Altana 用設施層級曝險上限得出 3,030 億美元。報告明確指出五份估算不可相加、也不能直接比較。

title: 路透：蘋果替中國市場訓練一套 AI 模型，阿里巴巴出手幫練
summary:
路透社週四引述消息人士獨家報導，蘋果已為中國市場訓練一套專屬的大型語言模型，訓練過程由阿里巴巴提供支援。這推翻 […]

〈路透：蘋果替中國市場訓練一套 AI 模型，阿里巴巴出手幫練〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
路透社週四引述消息人士獨家報導，蘋果已為中國市場訓練一套專屬的大型語言模型，訓練過程由阿里巴巴提供支援。這推翻了蘋果過去在中國只借用第三方模型的做法，也讓蘋果可望成為第一家獲北京放行、能在中國提供自有 AI 模型的外國公司。至於 Apple Intelligence 的生成式 AI 備案，早在 7 月中就已通過中國網信辦註冊，屆時將由阿里巴巴的通義千問與百度技術一起搭配上陣。
（前情提要：蘋果 Apple Intelligence 獲准登陸中國！整合阿里、百度大模型，股價狂飆創歷史新高）
（背景補充：北京擬管制自家 AI 模型出口，Qwen、豆包、Z.ai 全被點名）
重點摘要
- 路透社獨家：蘋果為中國市場自訓大型語言模型，阿里巴巴提供訓練支援
- 蘋果可望成首家獲北京批准、在中國提供自有 AI 模型的外國企業
- Apple Intelligence 已於 7 月通過網信辦備案，將隨 iOS 更新在中國推出
蘋果在中國的 AI 佈局再度取得進度。路透社週四引述知情人士報導，蘋果已經替中國市場訓練了一套專屬的大型語言模型，而訓練工作由阿里巴巴出手支援。
這件事的重點不在於蘋果又找了一個中國夥伴，而在於做法變了。蘋果過去在中國的策略是直接採用當地業者的現成模型，畢竟 ChatGPT 與 Claude 這些美國模型在中國本來就不能用。現在蘋果選擇自己訓練一套。
外企首張「自有模型通行證」
若順利落地，蘋果將成為第一家獲北京批准、可在中國提供自有 AI 模型的外國公司。這在中國是相當罕見的鬆口，當地對演算法與模型的審查向來看得很緊，境外業者要把自家模型端上檯面幾乎沒有前例。
值得玩味的是這套模型的養成方式。名義上是蘋果的自有模型，實際的訓練支援卻來自阿里巴巴，等於蘋果出題目、阿里當教練。對一家向來把核心技術牢牢抓在手上的公司來說，這是不小的妥協，也是進入中國市場必須付的過路費。
蘋果與阿里巴巴皆未回應此事件，中國網信辦除了完成服務註冊之外也沒有進一步說明。
常見問題
蘋果為什麼要專門為中國訓練一套模型？
因為 ChatGPT、Claude 等美國模型在中國無法使用，蘋果過去只能採用當地業者的現成模型。自訓模型讓蘋果拿回一定的技術主導權，也可望成為首家獲北京批准在中國提供自有 AI 模型的外國公司。
中國版 Apple Intelligence 用的是哪些技術？
由三套技術組成：蘋果自訓的中國專屬模型、阿里巴巴通義千問負責語言理解與生成、百度負責搜尋相關功能。該服務已於 7 月通過中國網信辦備案，預計未來幾個月隨 iOS 更新推出。

title: NUSD 為何沒有脫錨？Neutrl 撤走 351 萬流動性，把 Curve 池列進黑名單
summary:
Neutrl 暫停 NUSD 鑄幣與贖回已超過一天，負面討論持續發酵，但這顆合成美元的價格幾乎沒動，目前仍守在 […]

〈NUSD 為何沒有脫錨？Neutrl 撤走 351 萬流動性，把 Curve 池列進黑名單〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
Neutrl 暫停 NUSD 鑄幣與贖回已超過一天，負面討論持續發酵，但這顆合成美元的價格幾乎沒動，目前仍守在 0.998 美元附近。動區實際上鏈查證發現，答案不在儲備，而在合約權限：團隊在台北時間 8 月 13 日晚間撤走 Curve 池內約 351 萬美元流動性，96 秒後就把該池地址寫進 NUSD 的 denylist，池子從此無法轉入、轉出與交換。沒有人能買賣，價格自然不會脫錨。
（前情提要：穩定幣 NUSD 贖回與造幣突喊停！儲備疑雲、法律顧問介入）
（背景補充：穩定幣 apxUSD 嚴重脫錨跌破 0.75 鎂！微策略 STRC 重挫 20% 引爆 RWA 抵押品危機）
重點摘要
- Neutrl 8/13 撤走 Curve NUSD/USDC 池約 351 萬美元，池內現僅剩約 2.7 萬美元
- 撤資後 96 秒，該 LP 池地址被寫進 NUSD 合約的 denylist，交易功能全數失效
- NUSD 現報約 0.998 美元、流通約 5,330 萬美元，價格穩定是因為無法交易
DeFi 協定 Neutrl 週四暫停 NUSD 鑄幣與贖回後，社群質疑聲量累積了十幾個小時，這顆合成美元卻始終沒有脫錨跡象。調閱以太坊鏈上紀錄後我們能發現原因。
NUSD 的主要流動性只有一個去處，就是部署在 Curve 上的 NUSD/USDC 池（0x7E19…3b09）。台北時間 8 月 13 日晚間 7 點 12 分，這個池子被一次提走 1,578,976 USDC 與 1,933,079 NUSD，換算約 351 萬美元，幾乎是整池的全部。
96 秒之後，也就是同日晚間 7 點 13 分 59 秒，地址 0xDE72…1504 對 NUSD 合約送出一筆 addToDenylist 交易，參數填的正是上面那個 Curve 池地址。再過十幾分鐘，Neutrl 官方才發出暫停公告。
Neutrl has temporarily paused minting, redemptions, and other protocol functions following circumstances affecting protocol reserves. These measures have been taken in the interest of our users, after advice from legal counsel, to preserve an orderly process while the impact is…
— Neutrl (@Neutrl) August 13, 2026
封鎖後池子等於被焊死
動區以公開節點呼叫 NUSD 合約的 isDenylisted 函式查詢該池地址，回傳值為 true，確認目前仍在名單上。NUSD 合約本身就寫有 addToDenylist、removeFromDenylist 與 DENYLIST_MANAGER_ROLE 等權限設計。
被列入 denylist 的地址，代幣的轉入與轉出都會被合約擋下。對一個 AMM 池來說，這代表存入、提出與交換三件事同時失效。截至發稿，該池僅剩約 14,876 顆 NUSD 與 12,151 USDC，合計約 2.7 萬美元。
要說明的是，黑名單功能在穩定幣裡並不罕見，USDT 與 USDC 都具備凍結地址的能力，通常用於配合執法或攔阻遭竊資產。這次引發爭議的不是功能存在，而是它被指向了自家的流動性池，且緊接在團隊撤走該池全部流動性之後。
根據 DefiLlama 數據，NUSD 目前報價約 0.9983 美元、流通規模約 5,330 萬美元。動區日前報導過，Neutrl 以「儲備受到未說明的情況影響」為由暫停協定功能，並基於法律建議停掉其他操作，連帶使結構化收益協定 Strata 暫停相關市場。截至截稿，Neutrl 尚未對撤走流動性與列入黑名單的操作提出說明。
常見問題
NUSD 為什麼沒有脫錨？
因為唯一的 Curve 流動性池在 8 月 13 日被撤走約 351 萬美元後，池子地址隨即被寫入 NUSD 合約的 denylist，轉入、轉出與交換功能全數失效。沒有交易發生，報價自然停在 0.998 美元附近。
穩定幣有黑名單功能正常嗎？
正常，USDT 與 USDC 都能凍結地址，多用於配合執法或攔阻被盜資金。爭議點在於 Neutrl 把名單用在自家流動性池上，時間點又緊接在撤走該池全部流動性之後，目前尚未說明原因。

title: 重啟核電公投拍板：11/28 併大選登場，非核家園迎全民攤牌
summary:
立法院今（14）日院會表決通過三項公投案，其中「重啟核電」公投確定與 11 月 28 日九合一大選合併舉行。 […]

〈重啟核電公投拍板：11/28 併大選登場，非核家園迎全民攤牌〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
立法院今（14）日院會表決通過三項公投案，其中「重啟核電」公投確定與 11 月 28 日九合一大選合併舉行。
（前情提要：賴清德拍板：核二核三「具重啟條件」，AI 時代臺灣電力缺口撐不住了）
（背景補充：臺電送審核三再運轉計畫「最快要 2 年」，核電廠全開能提供臺灣多少電力？）
立法院院會今（14）日以 59 比 51 的表決結果，拍板通過「重啟核電」公投主文，與「鞭刑」、「交通罰鍰專款專用」兩案一起成案，確定於 11 月 28 日九合一大選當天合併投票。
這場攻防原本喊出六案齊發，最終在野黨團聯手精簡為三案闖關，其中重啟核電這一票，牽動的不只是電價與供電穩定，還有攸關 AI 資料中心用電胃口的能源政策走向。
根據聯合新聞網報導，國民黨團起初端出的版本洋洋灑灑，把健康、供電、電價、國防韌性與 AI 產業發展五大訴求全塞進主文；歷經 14 日院會協商大幅瘦身後，拍板定案的題目濃縮成一句話：
「你是否支援政府使用『核電』振興經濟，以廢除『非核家園』的能源政策？」
這道題目隨後在藍白陣營的人數優勢下完成表決，正式取得成案門票。
最終闖關的三案
這場表決端上檯面的公投提案原先多達六項，歷經協商冷凍期與席次盤算後，最終只有三案順利闖關，其餘三案則在協商桌上出局：
- 過關：國民黨團主推的「重啟核電」、「鞭刑」，以及「交通罰鍰專款專用」
- 出局：國民黨團的「反廢死」，加上民眾黨團提出的「移轉投票」、「安樂死」
出局的三案中，民眾黨團的兩項提案主要卡在沒能取得國民黨團奧援；黨團盤算年底投票若塞進太多題目，恐怕稀釋動員能量、拉長排隊時間，因此協調過程中主動割捨，集中火力衝剩下三案。
不過即使闖過立法院這關，戰役也還沒結束。公投案要真正生效，同意票必須跨過 488 萬 7,133 票的法定門檻，且同意票還得多於不同意票。
「非核家園」政策究竟會不會被翻轉，最終還是得看 11 月 28 日開票結果。
AI 用電缺口成攻防焦點，黃仁勳效應仍在發酵
支援這項公投的一方主張，核能議題早已跨越藍綠界線，不再只是特定政黨的立場。他們引用臺灣勵志協會（TIA）做的一份最新調查作為佐證，數字顯示全臺有 79% 的受訪者傾向支援核四重新啟用，被解讀為民眾普遍擔心供電吃緊、電價持續墊高。
提案方也主張，隨著科學研究與國際能源趨勢演進，當年訂下非核家園的理由，已經跟不上台灣現階段在國安與經濟層面的實際需求。
值得注意的是，國民黨團原始提案主文明白列出「支援人工智慧（AI）產業發展」作為訴求之一，這也點出這場公投背後真正的變數：AI 資料中心持續擴張，台灣的電力缺口正在加速浮現。
輝達執行長黃仁勳去年在核三重啟公投前夕來臺，也公開喊出「核能更好」，將核電與 AI 工廠產能直接掛鉤；台灣是否具備足夠且穩定的供電能力，攸關能否持續吃下 AI 供應鏈的龐大訂單。
非核家園走到十字路口，去年公投才剛未過關
這不是核三重啟第一次交付全民公投。2025 年 8 月 23 日，核三重啟公投就曾投票表決，儘管同意票數多於不同意票，但最終未跨過法定門檻，公投未能透過。
時隔一年，重啟核電議題再度捲土重來，且這次直接鎖定廢除「非核家園」政策本身，訴求層級更高。
今年 3 月，總統賴清德已鬆口表示核二、核三廠「具備重啟條件」；台電也已將核三廠再運轉計畫送交主管機關審查，最快仍需約 2 年才能完成程式。
外界解讀，這場 11 月 28 日的公投結果雖不會直接決定核電廠何時恢復發電，但將是觀察臺灣能源政策是否真正轉向的重要指標。
